title: Maryland Counties: ADA Title II PDF Accessibility, 9 Measured | SignalFeed.dev
description: How Maryland counties of 50,000+ stand on PDF accessibility before the April 26, 2027 ADA Title II date: 34% of 370 sampled PDFs untagged, 10% scanned. Aggregate, automated signals.
h1: Maryland: Title II PDF backlog in counties of 50,000+
body:
Maryland has 16 counties of 50,000 or more residents with an official website listed in Wikidata. Under the ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35, subpart H), a county's date depends on its population in the most recent decennial Census: 50,000 or more means April 26, 2027. Web content, PDFs included, must conform to WCAG 2.1 Level AA, subject to the rule's exceptions. Smaller counties, cities and special districts in Maryland have until April 26, 2028 under the current rule.

Does ADA Title II apply to Maryland?

Yes. Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act is federal law and covers every state and local government in every state: Maryland's state agencies, counties, cities, towns, school districts and special districts. The 2024 web rule adds technical requirements for their websites, apps and the documents they post (WCAG 2.1 Level AA). Its compliance date depends on population: April 26, 2027 for governments serving 50,000 or more people, April 26, 2028 for smaller ones and for special districts. This is general information, not legal advice.

We measured the PDFs these counties link from their public websites. This page summarizes Maryland as a whole. It does not name or rank individual counties. For cities, see the city Backlog Index.

Maryland at a glance

  • 9 of 16 counties measured with a usable sample (20 or more PDFs). The rest blocked automated visitors, host documents on other systems, or had too few PDFs to sample; that is not a clean result.
  • 370 PDFs analyzed. 34.3% had no accessibility tags, lower than the national figure of 45.1%. 10.3% were scanned images with no usable text, and 45.7% did not declare a document language.
  • 0 of 27 sampled PDFs passed the veraPDF PDF/UA-1 checks.
  • The median measured county has roughly 1,100 pages of PDFs failing at least one basic check; across the measured counties that is on the order of 38,000 pages.
  • 49% of the sampled PDFs were modified in 2024 or later. Recent documents are more likely to still be in active use, and documents used to apply for, access or participate in a service are not covered by the rule's exception for preexisting documents.

What this means for a Maryland county

An untagged PDF gives a screen reader no headings, no reading order and no table structure. A scanned PDF gives it nothing at all. Both typically fail WCAG 2.1 AA (for example 1.3.1 Info and Relationships, and for scans 1.1.1 Non-text Content), and both are common in agendas, minutes, budgets and forms.

Not every old PDF has to be fixed. The rule exempts archived web content and preexisting conventional electronic documents unless they are currently used to apply for, access or participate in a service. The practical order is usually: fix the export settings so new documents are born accessible, remediate forms and anything people use to get a service, and move true archives to a clearly marked archive section. Our ADA Title II PDF guide walks through it.

For agendas, minutes and notices, our accessible meeting templates for small public bodies ($24, Word + PDF/UA) export tagged PDFs from Word, so new documents start out accessible.

What this is, and what it isn't

These are automated signals, not a conformance evaluation. An automated check can show that a PDF fails; it cannot show that a PDF conforms. Estimates are scaled from samples, and a few very long documents can move a number a lot. The full method is on the national Backlog Index page.
